English Martyrs
ING-glish MAR-ters
noun (church history)
From English + martyr (Greek martys, a witness); the Protestant believers burned in England, chiefly under Mary Tudor, for the recovered gospel.

📖 Biblical Definition

The English Martyrs are the Protestant believers who were burned, hanged, or otherwise put to death in England for the recovered gospel, most of them in the brief and bloody reign of Mary Tudor (1553–58), whom history remembers as "Bloody Mary." Some three hundred were burned in less than four years — bishops and plowmen, scholars and women, the famous and the unknown. William Tyndale had already been strangled and burned abroad for giving England the Bible; under Mary the fires came home. Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, and Nicholas Ridley — the Oxford martyrs — were burned for denying the Mass and confessing justification by faith. Latimer comforted Ridley in the flames with words England never forgot: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out." Their stories were gathered by John Foxe in his Acts and Monuments — the "Book of Martyrs" — which next to the Bible shaped English piety for generations. This dictionary honors the English Martyrs as faithful witnesses who counted Christ and His truth dearer than their own lives, fulfilling the Lord's word that the faithful unto death receive the crown of life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Protestant believers burned in England for the gospel, chiefly under Mary Tudor ("Bloody Mary," 1553–58) — some three hundred, including the Oxford martyrs Cranmer, Latimer, and Ridley. Their witness, gathered in Foxe's Book of Martyrs, shaped English piety for centuries.

ENGLISH MARTYRS, noun. The Protestant believers put to death in England for the recovered gospel.

Most were burned under Mary Tudor ("Bloody Mary"), 1553–1558 — some three hundred in under four years.

The Oxford martyrs — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley — burned for denying the Mass.

Latimer's word in the fire: "we shall this day light such a candle... as I trust shall never be put out."

Their accounts gathered in John Foxe's Acts and Monuments, the "Book of Martyrs."

📖 Key Scripture

Rev 2:10 — "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

Matt 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

Heb 11:35 — "others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The age that prizes comfort cannot imagine dying for a doctrine, and so it recasts the English Martyrs as victims of political intolerance rather than witnesses to truth; the deeper corruption is to forget that they died for the very gospel a comfortable church now treats as negotiable.

expand to see more

The modern world reads the English Martyrs through the lens of religious liberty and tolerance, as if their tragedy were merely that people once killed over religion. There is truth in lamenting the cruelty. But to stop there is to miss the point of their death: they did not die for tolerance; they died for justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, and the rejection of the Mass — the gospel itself. They "loved not their lives unto the death" (Rev 12:11) because they loved Christ more.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historical record, preserved in Foxe. The principle to recover is the costliness of the truth they died for. A church that treats the doctrines of grace and the gospel of faith alone as matters indifferent has forgotten that men were burned to recover them. "Fear not them which kill the body" (Matt 10:28): the English Martyrs feared God more than the fire, and their candle, by God's grace, was never put out.

From Greek martys (witness); the Protestant believers burned in England, chiefly under Mary Tudor, whose witness Foxe gathered in the Book of Martyrs.
